question: Can a Muslim pass on haram gifts like wine or pork to non-Muslim friends and family?
asked: He is a convert in Geneva working in a position (sales or similar) where it is customary to receive many gifts from his company and other companies. Sometimes these gifts are haram, such as sausage or wine. As a convert he has plenty of non-Muslim friends and even siblings. Can he pass this haram merchandise on to them, without selling it, simply giving it to them to benefit from, since he will not partake of it himself?
answer:
Brother Nicholas, you ask a very good question. This is supposed to be a rapid round, but at the same time this is a question that is a bit technical, believe it or not. There are two opinions on this issue amongst the classical 'ulama, amongst the early madhahib, so just FYI, very quickly, I'll try to summarize them.

The issue really is a very technical one, and that is: are non-Muslims also obliged to follow the laws of the Shari'ah, or are they exempt from the laws of the Shari'ah? In other words, are they going to be punished for not obeying the laws of the Shari'ah, in which case there is no way that you can help them towards that punishment? Or are they absolved from the minutiae, not mukallaf (that is the technical term) by the laws of the Shari'ah? This is the usuli controversy that goes back to early Islam.

The majority position, the Shafi'i school, the Hanbali school and the Maliki school, say that non-Muslims are indeed obligated to follow the details of the law. And therefore, generally speaking, they would say that it is not allowed in any way, fashion or form for any Muslim, by any means, to make it convenient for a non-Muslim to do something that would be haram in our own Shari'ah. And there is no question that that is the better and the safer opinion. The other school of law, the Hanafi school, said that non-Muslims are not obliged to follow the minutiae of our Shari'ah; they're not obliged to follow the details of the law. And therefore they are a bit more lax in some of these areas, allowing non-Muslims to benefit from that which might be haram for us.

Now, as for the majority opinion, there are lots of evidences for it. Allah says in the Qur'an: "Do not cooperate together in any sin or any injustice." And if it is a sin for us, it's a sin for others, so we should not cooperate. So that position would be that we should simply destroy the wine and throw away the sausage or pork, get rid of the silk, whatever it might be, and do nothing with it. And our Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has forbidden the selling of alcohol, and of dead animals, and of pig, and of idols."

Now, your question was not about selling; your question was about simply passing it on. And the majority would argue that just as we're not allowed to sell it and get the money, so too we would not be allowed to gift it. That's what they would say: if we're not allowed to sell, we're not allowed to gift either. And in fact, there is an authentic hadith in this regard, reported in Imam Ahmad's Musnad and others, narrated from Ibn Abbas, that a man (believe it or not, this is a shocking hadith to most Muslims when they hear it) gifted the Prophet ﷺ a sealed canister of alcohol, khamr. The Prophet said, "Do you not know that Allah has made it haram?" The man said no. He was a new Muslim. He didn't know any better, coming from whatever faraway place, and he wanted to give something expensive, so he brought a bottle of wine. Or not a bottle, and obviously not a glass, but a canister of wine. Can you believe somebody gifted the Prophet a canister of wine? Because he didn't know any better. The man didn't know.

So the first thing the Prophet ﷺ said was, "Do you know that it is haram? Do you not know?" And the man said, "No, I didn't." So he's forgiven, because he didn't know any better. Now, another man whispered something in his ear. The Prophet ﷺ said, "What did you whisper to him?" And the man said, "I told him that he cannot gift it to you, but he should sell it." In other words, the second man, whoever he was (we don't know his name), is basically trying to get him out of an awkward situation and saying, "Look, take your gift back and just go sell it." Our Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah has forbidden its drinking, He has forbidden its selling as well." Beautiful hadith. The same Being who made the drinking of it haram has made the selling of it haram. And so when the man heard this, he took the bottle, opened it up, and just poured it into the street. Khalas, I'm not going to have anything to do with this. And there is no question, dear brother, that that is the default, and the better and the purer ruling: just get rid of it. Do not do anything with it.

That having been said, do realize there is a dissenting madhhab out there, the Hanafi madhhab, and they actually do have some evidence for this. For example, in the famous hadith in Sahih Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, our Prophet ﷺ gifted 'Umar ibn al-Khattab silk, and 'Umar said, "How can I wear it?" He said, "I didn't gift it to you to wear; it's not meant for you to wear." So 'Umar could have gifted it to his wives. Instead, he decided to gift it to his mushrik brother in Makkah. This hadith is in Bukhari and Muslim. Now, this hadith has been interpreted in many different ways, but it is clear to many scholars that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab understood: "I can't wear silk, but my brother is a non-Muslim; he can wear silk, so I might as well gift it to him." So he gifted it to his brother as a non-Muslim. And Ibn Taymiyyah also remarked that it is permissible to gift silk to a non-Muslim, even if the Muslim himself cannot wear it. Based upon this, they derived that the non-Muslim is not obliged to follow the details of the Shari'ah. And so some scholars would allow you to pass on material that is not allowed for you to non-Muslims.

Among the evidences that are mentioned as well is one in the early book of Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam, the Book of Amwal, the book of money, where he has an interesting narration that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab was collecting the kharaj, which is a type of special tax collected from the non-Muslims. And they gave him pig and they gave him wine; they had a lot of that merchandise. So he's collecting the kharaj, which is a type of tax. I mean, again, not tax; the taxation system of early Islamic Shari'ah is very different, but for our sake, let's call it a type of tax. And so they gave bottles of wine and pork, because that's what they had, and they gave it to him as the state collecting taxes. So the person in charge came back to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and said, "They gave this; what do I do now? This is khamr and this is pig." So 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said, "Go back and tell them to sell the wine and the pork, and then give us the money."

Now here, if a Muslim had given wine and pork, nobody would say, "Go sell it and then give us the money"; it's haram for a Muslim to do. But 'Umar ibn al-Khattab radiyAllahu 'anhu basically said to that community, "Look, we cannot accept that, but you guys do it." And so he benefited from the money for the treasury, but he didn't take the actual substances. And again, the point here, once again, is that non-Muslims can do what we cannot do, and we're allowed to basically facilitate: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab told them to do this, and then they did it. And Ibn Taymiyyah remarks on this incident: "And this is well known, and it is confirmed from 'Umar, and it is the position of the famous scholars."

So based on these types of narrations, one group of scholars did say... And by the way, there's another argument that is used, which is an interesting argument, and that is a Muslim man married to a Kitabi lady, a Jewish or Christian lady. It is understood that the lady is going to go shopping with his money, and it is understood that she's going to purchase things that are haram for him but halal for her. Especially in early Christianity, and in the Catholic Church till our days, they drink wine as part of their rituals. And therefore this group of 'ulama argued that the husband is not able to stop his wife. That's her right: she's going to have wine, even in the house, and she's going to be drinking it for her rituals, and even otherwise, as it is halal for her to drink, meaning from her Shari'ah perspective, not in our Shari'ah.

And again, there is a gray area. Some of the scholars are stricter, and they would say that she should not buy it from his money; there are opinions even like this. And then the counter-response is: well, no, if he's the husband, then he has to maintain her basic daily routine, and if her Christian rituals state that she must drink that cup... because again, the Christian rituals, the Catholic rituals, do have the consecration of the wine. So again, this is a gray area. And one group of scholars did say that the Christian lady, or the Jewish lady, is going to be purchasing haram under the umbrella of the husband, literally using the credit card of the husband, metaphorically. And so this indicates that with non-Muslims, we can basically turn the other way. And if you follow that paradigm, then that group of scholars would say that you can just pass on the stuff. You are obviously not allowed to eat or drink anything that is haram, or wear anything haram, but if you give it to others among the non-Muslims, your siblings or your roommates, for example...

Now, what I would advise you to do is definitely to follow the majority position and get rid of it. That having been said, if you have roommates, for example... And here also, by the way, my position is that you cannot compare silk with pork with alcohol. These are three separate levels of hurmah, if you like, of tahrim; three separate levels of evil. And the evils of alcohol are the worst. And there is no question, in my opinion (this is the least that can be said), that it is strongly discouraged, if not outright haram, and I'm very sympathetic to the majority position, to give somebody alcohol. However, silk: the level of tahrim of silk is not the same. And so 'Umar gifting his brother silk indicates that silk is something much easier to deal with. And as for pork, it is in between the two. If your roommate sees it and eats it, and he knows you're not going to eat it, okay, you didn't push the plate in his direction; you turned a blind eye. Inshallah, then I can see where you're coming from in that regard.

But definitely, dearest brother, **when it comes to alcohol, simply get rid of it.** Pour it down. Do not aid other people in the drinking of alcohol in any way, fashion or form. That is definitely something that should be avoided, because Allah has cursed khamr and everything to do with khamr, so we don't want to get involved with it whatsoever. And as for the other items that you get that are not alcohol, it is much easier to follow an 'Umari position, if you get my drift here. And if you were to follow the majority, it is safer for you. And Allah knows best.
